summary: Sets out a Bill of Rights for people and organizations that appear in public directory listings. It is informational and was replaced by RFC 1417. Note that the abstract recorded in some indexes does not match the title.

plainLanguage.summary: This 1992 document is a short bill of rights for people whose details appear in a public electronic directory. It lists seven rights, from the right not to be listed at all to the right to have mistakes fixed quickly. It was later replaced.

subtitle: Rights for people listed in public directories.

tldr.problem: Public directories held information about people with no safeguards for accuracy or privacy.
tldr.mechanism: The North American Directory Forum sets out seven user rights: not to be listed, to be informed when listed, to see your entry, to correct errors, to remove information, to have your privacy protected by law, and to have these rights fulfilled promptly.
tldr.outcome: Replaced by RFC 1417, this early standard formalized privacy expectations in networked directories.

today: The unit metadata records RFC 1295 as Informational and obsoleted by RFC 1417. As the RFC itself notes, it is a near-verbatim copy of an NADF document; it represents an early effort to establish privacy norms in electronic directories.

sections.title: Introduction and Purpose
sections.content:
This RFC is a near-verbatim copy of a document known as NADF-265, produced by the North American Directory Forum (NADF). The Forum is a collection of service providers that plan to offer a cooperative directory service in North America by interconnecting electronic directories using the CCITT X.500 series of standards.

To address security and privacy issues, the Forum introduces a User Bill of Rights for entries in the Public Directory. The rights apply to the Public Directory, the portion meant for public dissemination; users may instead list information in a private directory, or in some combination of the two.
sections.plainLanguage: Before you put your name in an electronic directory, here are the rights you should have. They cover the part of the directory anyone can see, not the private parts.

sections.title: The Seven User Rights
sections.content: The Bill of Rights lists seven rights for a user. A user has: (I) the right not to be listed; (II) the right to have the user or the user's agent informed when the entry is created; (III) the right to examine the entry; (IV) the right to correct inaccurate information; (V) the right to remove specific information from the entry; (VI) the right to be assured that the listing complies with US or Canadian law regulating privacy or access to information; and (VII) the right to expect timely fulfillment of these rights.
sections.plainLanguage: You can say no to being listed, be told when your entry appears, read it, fix mistakes, remove things you want private, rely on privacy law, and expect it all to happen fast.

sections.title: Scope and Context
sections.content: The rights pertain to the Public Directory. The RFC explains that when an entry is listed in the Directory, that information can be accessed unless restricted by security and privacy controls. A user, or a user's agent, may elect to list information in the Public Directory, a private directory, or some combination; for example, a user might publicly list a telephone number or an electronic mail address and designate other information for specific private use.
sections.plainLanguage: These rules apply to the part of the directory that is open to the public. Other parts can be restricted, and you can choose what goes where.

references.text: North American Directory Forum, User Bill of Rights for entries and listings in the Public Directory, NADF-265, January 1992.
